articles.title: Minneapolis progressives turn on George Floyd-era public safety overhaul, push to dismantle office
articles.summary: Minneapolis Council leaders propose eliminating the Office of Community Safety over audit failures and wasteful spending, and Mayor Jacob Frey pushes back.
articles.body: Minneapolis City Council leaders advanced a proposal Tuesday to eliminate the city's Office of Community Safety as part of a sweeping public safety restructuring, citing poor management and financial oversight concerns. Mayor Jacob Frey warned the move could jeopardize critical services. According to The Star Tribune, the office was created by Mayor Frey in 2022 in response to calls for police reform after the death of George Floyd. 3 DEAD, INCLUDING SUSPECTED GUNMAN, AND 3 OFFICERS INJURED IN MINNEAPOLIS SHOOTING City Council President Elliott Payne and Council Member Robin Wonsley, who are spearheading the measure to eliminate the office, cited performance and cost concerns in a statement to FOX 9. "It is good governance to stop investing in things that are not producing meaningful outcomes and are wasting taxpayer dollars," Wonsley said. "The Office of Community Safety has also contributed to increased audit costs due to poor management. It’s our responsibility to cut unnecessary bureaucracy that does not contribute to public safety." The proposal marks a significant reversal for a city that reorganized public safety operations after Floyd's death. Frey, who established the office in 2022, criticized council members for seeking to dismantle a structure some had previously championed. In a statement to Fox News Digital, the mayor warned that the proposed elimination could threaten existing public safety programs. "This office — one that these council members advocated for — manages services like mental health response, violence prevention and police reform. If council members want these services in jeopardy, that’s on them. This wholesale elimination without a plan, combined with other proposed cuts to MPD, is not a serious proposal when it comes to public safety in our city," Frey said. According to the City of Minneapolis, the Office of Community Safety oversees five departments: police, fire, 911, emergency management and neighborhood safety. The office was designed to coordinate public safety services, improve communication between departments and establish a unified chain of command and accountability. GOP ACCUSES WALZ ALLIES OF BURYING $52M MEDICAID FRAUD REPORT BEFORE ELECTION The proposal comes amid mounting scrutiny of the city's violence prevention spending. A recent Minneapolis audit identified serious deficiencies in the Neighborhood Safety Department's oversight of community-based violence prevention contracts, including inadequate documentation and financial controls that increased the risk of fraud and misuse of taxpayer money. According to the investigation, the city failed to properly oversee millions of dollars awarded to violence prevention organizations. The audit examined a system that has directed more than $36 million to five major violence prevention programs since 2023. WALZ ADMINISTRATION IGNORED FRAUD WARNINGS AS BILLIONS VANISHED, HOUSE OVERSIGHT REPORT ALLEGES Payne defended the proposed restructuring as a way to preserve services while reducing administrative expenses. "These proposed changes to the government structure ensure that progress on issues such as public safety and racial disparities is not impacted by unnecessary costs and bureaucratic bottlenecks," Payne told FOX 9. "Now more than ever, our city government must be responsive to the needs of residents, and its structure should reflect that." The city's published 2026 public safety budget allocated more than $16 million to the Office of Community Safety, nearly $10 million to Neighborhood Safety and more than $225 million to the Minneapolis Police Department. It remains unclear how much money eliminating the office would actually save. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Wonsley defended the proposal in comments to Fox News Digital, explaining that key non-police programs that continue to show success, such as the Behavioral Crisis Response team, predated the Office of Community Safety and would continue to operate without it. "The Office of Community Safety became administrative bloat that was a barrier to creating and expanding alternative responses rather than leading the development of a comprehensive public safety system," Wonsley said. She argued the $2 million office had become a "bureaucratic barrier" plagued by mismanagement by Mayor Frey and said taxpayers have paid the price. "The city can advance a comprehensive safety system and support police reform much more efficiently without unnecessary bureaucratic layers that have proven to be ineffective," Wonsley added. "Residents should not anticipate negative impacts because OCS was never able to effectively manage or oversee programs and services. The proposal does not eliminate any violence prevention or public safety programs that produce results. It simply removes administrative bloat."

articles.body: NEW DELHI: India and the US are heading towards a landing point on the trade deal that they have been negotiating for over 18 months, Union external affairs minister S Jaishankar said on Wednesday reviving optimism about the successful conclusion of the ongoing talks soon.Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman had suggested earlier this month there was a deadlock in the talks, with both sides reaching a point where it would be difficult to concede any further ground. My sense is that this is an issue which is heading towards a landing point."Earlier this month, USTRJamieson Greer said the US and India were working to finalise the agreement but it was not imminent.Jaishankar also spoke about Washington's new approach to economic engagement. articles.title: Warning to women amid shortages of some HRT products
articles.summary: Two brands of HRT patches, including Estradot transdermal and FemSeven Conti patches, have been affected, the Department of Health has said.
articles.body:
Women have been warned against self-medicating to manage menopause symptoms amid a shortage of some Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT) medications.

Pharmacist Paul Irvine said he understood that women "are concerned" but urged them to speak to their GP or local chemist who could advise them about alternatives.

The warning follows official confirmation from the Department of Health that supplies of two major HRT patch brands have been disrupted.

The affected products include Estradot transdermal and FemSeven Conti, both of which are currently facing manufacturing or distribution delays.

Irvine, a pharmacy manager in Belfast, said much of the time with HRT medications, women often become comfortable with a particular brand.

"When they are short and they like to try alternatives, they may suffer side effects or it might just not work as well," he said.

"So it is important for us as pharmacists that we are there to guide people and offer them alternative and the correct advice."

Dr Ursula Mason, chair of the Royal College of General Practitioners Northern Ireland, said finding a substitute "can cause real anxiety for patients".

"This can be particularly so for HRT medication when a woman has found a preparation that works well for them," she said.

"Patients can be assured that the protocol in place only allows a substitution for exactly the same active ingredient at the same dose.

"If a woman finds that for whatever reason the new formulation is not managing their symptoms or they are having side effects, it would be important that they contact their GP to discuss both their symptoms and the options available around suitable alternatives."

The Department of Health said it was aware of "supply disruptions" affecting some HRT medications across the UK, including ongoing issues with Estradot transdermal patches and a more recent disruption affecting FemSeven Conti patches.

"Communications have been issued to healthcare professionals regarding the products affected, including advice on suitable alternatives that remain available," it said.

It added: "Serious Shortage Protocol (SSPs) for Estradot transdermal patches are currently in place until 8 January 2027, permitting pharmacists to supply alternative products to patients without the need for a new prescription, where the patient has agreed to this.

"If patients cannot access their prescribed medication or have concerns about an alternative, they should speak to a healthcare professional for advice about their treatment options."

Roisin Hillman, co-founder of Menopause Together, Northern Ireland's first menopause support charity, noted some women forced to switch brands due to medication shortages have reported side effects like itchy skin or patches falling off.

She said that ongoing HRT patch shortages are deeply frustrating for women. Once they find a medication that works, it often falls in short supply.

"This is an issue going on for years," she said advising women to request longer-term prescriptions from their GPs to stay ahead of supply gaps.

She also warned against sharing HRT with others.

"It is also really important that if you do have a shortage, and you can't get your normal HRT, to make sure you go back to your doctor.

"Please do not share HRT with other women because what is prescribed to you may not suit someone else so it is very important that you go back to your GP," she said.

"I know that when women have that fear and anxiety that the HRT they are on is helping so many aspects of their life and in particular a woman's mental health.

"If she on HRT that works for her and then if she is not getting that HRT it can be really hard."

articles.title: How a Chinese-made toy gets to a US retailer
articles.summary: With Christmas on the horizon, we trace children's toys from factories in China to US shelves.
articles.body:
On the underside of most children's toys on sale in the US you'll find the same three words – "Made in China".

Nearly eight in 10 toys (78.3%) imported into the country in 2024 came from China, according to US government figures.

Last year, toys imported from China were worth $9.8bn (£7.4bn), trade figures show.

With Christmas on the horizon, the toy industry in the US and elsewhere is about to have its busiest time of the year by far.

As retailers prepare their stocks for the festive rush, be they online giants or "mom-and-pop" physical stores, the BBC World Service's Follow the Money series traces how a toy gets from a factory in China to the US. And where the money goes.

Guangdong province, which neighbours Hong Kong in southern China, is the heart of the country's toy manufacturing industry.

In the city of Dongguan workers on the floor of the Mihox factory pop plastic toys out of steel moulds, and pile them into crates ready for painting.

The company says it employs more than 800 people and makes around 55 million toys a year for the American market, which represents half of its business.

Follow the money: The journey of a $30 toy from China to America

Every toy starts with a design from a customer, such as an American toy company. The factory then makes a prototype, and builds moulds from which plastic parts and other components are formed.

Going from the first idea to finished toy takes one to two years, says Melanie Wang from the Mihox sales team. Much of that is the customer going back to the drawing board. "They modified the design again, again, and again to improve it."

Once the design is signed off, things move more quickly. A mould takes about a month to make, and the production run lasts about three months.

So, how much of the US retail price does the factory get? "About 20%," says Wang.

On a $30 toy, that's $6, which has to cover the price of the plastic and other materials, production costs including wages, and what profit the factory makes.

Chinese factories typically make a profit of between 3% and 10%, according to Jay Foreman, chief executive of US toy firm Basic Fun. So for a $30 toy that's between 60 and 18 cents of the $6 the factory charges to make it.

Samson Ko is president of the Toys Manufacturers' Association of Hong Kong. Many of his members moved their factories across the border into mainland China in the 1980s, attracted by cheaper land and labour.

He says the way toys are made has barely changed since then. "Automation now takes place mostly in the moulding and the packaging process. But for soft toys, or even some of the electronics nowadays, it's still very labour intensive."

And Chinese labour isn't cheap anymore, he adds, after recent rises.

Average pay in Vietnam is about half of that in China, said one report at the start of this year.

Yet fewer than 10% of Ko's members have moved any production outside China, and in those cases mostly only because customers asked them to do so.

The Chinese factories remain busy, he says, because a single toy can undergo more than one manufacturing process, from moulding the parts, to adding electronics, sewing materials, and final assembly. This often requires it travelling to different factories.

Ko adds that in Guangdong these separate facilities are located close to each other, and used to "working in harmony". He says this makes the whole manufacturing process run more smoothly than in other countries.

From the factory, the toy goes by truck to a port, such as Shenzhen, the biggest in Guangdong.

Ivy Tse is co-founder of FreightAmigo, a Hong Kong logistics company that runs an online platform for both Hong Kong and mainland China exporters. These businesses can book a cargo container, sea passage to an overseas destination, arrange insurance cover, and secure finance.

Tse says it takes about 15 days for a cargo ship to get from Shenzhen to the US west coast, and 25 to 30 days to the east coast. This year's Christmas toys left China in August and September.

Freight, from factory to the US, usually adds about 10% to the manufacturing cost of a toy, adds Tse. So if we stick to a toy that retails for $30 in the US, and therefore costs $6 to make in China, the cost of getting it to the states is 60 cents.

Once the toy reaches the US there is currently a tariff on Chinese toys that has to be paid to the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP).

Following talks between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping last month, the two governments have recommended toys for lower tariffs. But no new rate or start date has been set, and the US must first hold a public consultation. For now the basic rate is 12.5%, and some toys pay more.

This is charged on the manufacturing price of the toy, not on how much it retails for. So for a $30 toy, that basic rate is 12.5% of $6, which is 75 cents.

This tariff is paid for by the American company that has imported the toys. One such firm is Learning Resources, a family business based near Chicago that sells educational toys. Half of these it imports from China.

"We pay 100% of the tariffs, let there be no doubt about that," says the company's chief executive Rick Woldenberg.

The cost of making the $30 toy, getting it to the US, and paying the import tariff, comes to $7.35. So that leaves $22.65, or 75.5% of the total.

That money never leaves the US, explains Foreman from Basic Fun. His firm, which is based in Florida, makes Tonka trucks and Care Bears cuddly toys.

"It's kept by my company, the [US] transportation company, the retailer," he says.

If we allow $2.65 for the US delivery firm, the toy company and the retailer will typically share the remaining revenues 50-50. So that would give them $10 each.

While profit margins are commercially sensitive and therefore not generally revealed, industry studies show that the toy firm and retailer would usually make a profit of up to 25% or $2.50.

Getting a toy onto the shelves in the US requires both a lot of work and a long journey.

articles.body: American Airlines has dropped flights to three destinations across the U.S., Mexico and the Middle East this year, leaving some travelers with fewer flight options. The airline has discontinued service to Santa Maria, California; Tijuana, Mexico; and Doha, Qatar, according to aviation outlet Simple Flying, which cited data from aviation analytics company Cirium. The cuts have left Santa Maria without service from a major U.S. legacy carrier, while Tijuana lost its only nonstop route operated by a U.S. airline. FURIOUS CROWDS PROTEST SKY-HIGH HOUSING COSTS AND MASS TOURISM IN MAJOR CITY By cutting its routes from Phoenix to Santa Maria and Tijuana, American Airlines has exited both destinations. At Santa Maria, Allegiant Air remains the only commercial airline serving the airport, with flights to Las Vegas, according to Simple Flying. Meanwhile, Qatar Airways has taken over the Philadelphia-to-Doha route, restoring nonstop service between the two cities after American's departure. Regarding the cancellation of service to Santa Maria, American Airlines said the decision was based on performance. American Airlines operated service to Santa Maria, California, under its American Eagle brand through a partnership with SkyWest Airlines, a spokesperson from the company told local outlet KEYT earlier this year. INNOCENT MISTAKE ON LONG FLIGHT COULD HAVE DEVASTATING CONSEQUENCES FOR TRAVELERS "Unfortunately, flights to SMX did not meet performance expectations, and SkyWest informed American it will discontinue service as of May 7," the official said. In June, American Airlines permanently cut its Philadelphia-to-Doha route after previously suspending flights due to regional hostilities, according to The Philadelphia Inquirer. The route failed to meet performance expectations. "As part of an optimization of our network and fleet, American has made the difficult decision to discontinue service to Doha, Qatar (DOH)," American Airlines spokesperson Bri Harper said in a statement to the outlet. In August, American Airlines discontinued service to Tijuana, Mexico, after the route failed to meet performance expectations. Steven Arroyo, an aviation safety expert and retired United Airlines captain based in Florida, told Fox News Digital that route cancellations are a common part of the airline business. "It's part of the economic reality of running an airline efficiently." Arroyo said travelers should monitor routes and ticket prices when planning upcoming trips. He encouraged travelers to "keep an eye on what's going on" with their planned routes and "do a little bit of research" before booking their trips.
